newsitem.title: UK: Crisis mounts as Queen Elizabeth ends holiday.
newsitem.headline: Crisis mounts as Queen Elizabeth ends holiday.

text.p: Queen Elizabeth returns from her annnual two-month holiday in Scotland on Tuesday to face a fresh scandal over the affairs and debts of her daughter-in-law, the flame-haired Duchess of York.
The queen dubbed 1992, the year when the marriages of two of her sons collapsed and the royal family's free-spending lifestyles were widely criticised, as her "annus horribilis".
But 1996, with divorces finalised for her two older sons and a series of scandalous stories in print, will surely not be remembered as one of the better years for the royal family.

After expensive divorce settlements to Diana, Princess of Wales, and the Duchess of York, the queen had hoped that the worst was over and was reported to be considering sweeping reforms to polish the tarnished image of the monarchy.

But sensational allegations about the duchess, popularly known as Fergie, and her relationships with several men in a book by a Greek psychic she consulted as well as her reportedly mounting debts have dominated British headlines.

Incensed by the latest scandal and the harm it may be doing to her granddaughters, the queen has reportedly drawn up a deal to settle the 36-year-old duchess's debts and to make her give up custody of her young daughters, Beatrice and Eugenie.
"The massive kiss-off would settle the Duchess of York's five million ($7.8 million) debts and pay for her to set up a new home in exile abroad," the top-selling Sun newspaper said.
Buckingham Palace refused to comment on the payoff report but a spokeswoman for the duchess said it was "ludicrous" and "absolute fabrication".
"It is absolute and utter rubbish," the spokeswoman said. "The Duchess is very hurt and upset by these stories, as any mother would be. She is completely devoted to her children."

Fergie's ex-husband Prince Andrew explained the terms of the deal, which would also include the loss of her title and promises that she would drop plans for her own autobiography or interviews, in a seven-hour meeting on Sunday, the Sun claimed.

In another setback last week, Fergie was forced to withdraw from a court case to try to block publication of another book by Allan Starkie, an associate of American financier John Bryan. Photographs of Bryan sucking the duchess's toes by a swimming pool in the south of France in 1992 caused a scandal in Britain.
Another newspaper reported that the queen had ordered a round-the-clock suicide watch on Fergie who was said to be distraught by the mounting personal attacks on her character.

Meanwhile, newly-divorced Prince Charles was having his own problems. His closest aide, Richard Aylard, will quit his job early next year leaving the prince to cope on his own as he embarks on a new life as a single man.

Buckingham Palace said the departure by Aylard, who has worked for the prince for 11 years, was mutally agreed but British media claim his departure was connected with the prince's confession of his adultery with Camilla Parker Bowles.

Intended to improve public sympathy for Charles, the confession about the heir to the throne's mistress backfired badly. It damaged the prince's public image and led to charges that he was unfit to be king. ($1=.6388 Pound)
